study_identification_part.si4_title: Neurofind: using deep learning to make individualised inferences in brain-based disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop and validate Neurofind, a freely available web-based tool that uses deep learning to provide individualized reports based on normative modeling from structural MRI images. The tool outputs two main metrics: (1) Outlier Index Score - deviation from normative brain morphology, and (2) Brain Age - predicted age based on brain morphometry, with exemplar applications in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Neuroharmony method - a random forest model that learns the relationship between image quality metrics (IQMs) and ComBat corrections, then predicts and applies corrections for new unseen images; trained twice (with age+sex covariates for Outlier Detection model, with sex covariate only for Brain Age model); designed specifically for harmonizing images from unseen scanners; within-scanner outlier removal performed before harmonization
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: Scanner effects on the ROIrel were mitigated using the Neuroharmony method [56]. Briefly, Neuroharmony uses a random forest model to capture the relationship between IQMs and the corrections for each brain region prescribed by ComBat, a popular harmonisation approach that uses an empirical Bayes framework to correct for additive and multiplicative batch effects [68]. Once this relationship is learned, Neuroharmony predicts and applies the ComBat corrections for a new set of IQMs extracted from an unseen T1-weighted image. Neuroharmony was trained twice to accommodate the specific needs of the Outlier Detection and Brain Age models. For the former, Neuroharmony was trained whilst controlling for the effects of age and sex, whereas for Brain Age, only sex was added as a covariate.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Outlier Index Score (OIS) - scaled reconstruction error from adversarial autoencoder representing number of interquartile ranges away from the median in the train set; categorized as Within the norm (<0.26), Low (≥0.26), Medium (≥1.1), and High (≥2.3) deviation; Brain Age Gap (BAG) - difference between predicted brain age and chronological age, normalized according to train set; region-specific OIS for each of 101 ROIs
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The manuscript clearly describes two main deviation metrics. The Outlier Index Score (OIS) is the scaled reconstruction error from the AAE, calculated as mean squared error between input and reconstruction, then scaled by subtracting the median and dividing by the IQR of the train set. Cut-offs for categorization were derived from quartiles of the train set OIS distribution. Brain Age Gap (BAG) is the standard metric of predicted age minus chronological age. Both overall and ROI-level OIS were calculated.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: The reconstruction error for each ROIrel was estimated by calculating the squared error between the inputted value and its reconstruction. An overall reconstruction error was then generated for each participant by calculating the mean squared error between the reconstruction and the inputted data. ... all values were scaled by subtracting the median and dividing by the interquartile range such that the median of the overall and ROI-level scaled errors was 0.0 (IQR = 1.0) ... The final scaled errors, which we named Outlier Index Score (OIS), represent the number of interquartile ranges away from the median in the train set. The OIS is categorised into: Within the norm (<0.26), Low ( ≥ 0.26), Medium ( ≥ 1.1) and High ( ≥ 2.3) deviations from the norm ... clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Independent-samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for group comparisons of overall and ROI-level OIS and BAG between patients and controls (normality tested with Shapiro-Wilk test); Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons in ROI-level analyses; Pearson's r or Spearman's rho for correlations between OIS/BAG and symptom severity depending on normality; symptom measures included MMSE for AD, SANS and SAPS (normalized and z-scored) for MCIC schizophrenia, PANSS for COBRE schizophrenia; mean pairwise cosine similarity calculated to quantify heterogeneity of deviations within groups across all ROIs and within predefined brain regions (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital lobes, insula, cingulate, subcortical structures, cerebellum, corpus callosum, ventricles); statistical significance set at 0.05; bootstrapping (1000 repetitions) used for confidence intervals of median differences
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Alzheimer's disease patients showed significantly larger overall deviations from normative brain morphology (55.2% with high deviations) particularly in temporal-limbic structures and ventricles, with greater homogeneity than controls; schizophrenia patients showed fewer extreme outliers (30.1%), with deviations mainly in hippocampus and pallidum and greater heterogeneity than controls; both groups showed signs of accelerated brain aging compared to matched healthy controls.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: In Alzheimer's disease (N=61), patients showed significantly larger overall Outlier Index Scores (median=2.46, IQR=2.50) compared to healthy controls (median=0.91, IQR=1.36; Mann-U=1361, p<0.001). Only 3.4% of AD patients had OIS within the normative range versus 25.9% of controls, with 55.2% of AD patients showing high deviations versus 13.8% of controls. Significantly larger ROI-level deviations were found bilaterally in amygdala, hippocampus, inferior temporal gyrus, and inferior lateral ventricle, and in left inferior parietal gyrus (all FDR-corrected p<0.05). AD severity (MMSE) was negatively correlated with deviations in left hippocampus (ρ=-0.28, p<0.05), left amygdala (ρ=-0.28, p<0.05), and left inferior temporal gyrus (ρ=-0.34, p<0.05). AD patients were more homogeneous than controls (mean cosine similarity 0.54±0.22 vs 0.31±0.25 across all ROIs), particularly in ventricles (0.72±0.20 vs 0.56±0.24) and subcortical regions (0.60±0.20 vs 0.42±0.20). Scaled BAG was significantly larger for AD (M=-0.1, SD=0.4) versus HC (M=-0.6, SD=0.4; p<0.001), indicating accelerated aging. In schizophrenia (N=134), there was no significant difference in overall OIS between patients (median=1.38, IQR=1.83) and controls (median=1.10, IQR=1.76; Mann-U=7657, p=0.091), though 30.1% of patients showed high deviations. Significant regional deviations were found in bilateral hippocampus and left putamen (FDR-corrected p<0.05). Right hippocampus deviations correlated with both positive (ρ=0.22, p<0.05) and negative (ρ=0.20, p<0.05) symptom severity. SZ patients were more heterogeneous than controls (mean cosine similarity 0.32±0.15 vs 0.40±0.17), most notably in ventricles (0.55±0.22 vs 0.62±0.23) and subcortical regions (0.38±0.20 vs 0.47±0.21). Scaled BAG was significantly larger for SZ (M=0.8, SD=0.5) versus HC (M=0.6, SD=0.4; p<0.01), with BAG correlating with positive symptoms (ρ=0.20, p<0.05) but not negative symptoms. Brain Age model achieved MAE of 10.0±6.3 years on external healthy controls.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The tool is not customizable for advanced users; designed for general-purpose transdiagnostic metrics rather than disorder-specific diagnosis or real-world clinical prediction; brain age model exhibits regression-to-mean bias (age bias) that requires covariate adjustment in further analyses; Neuroharmony effectiveness depends on image quality metrics falling within expected range; may not be suitable for subjects outside training range (ages 20-80, non-white ethnicities, non-1.5T/3T scanners); results should not be used for clinical decisions as this is a research tool; less clear-cut results for schizophrenia reflect the heterogeneous nature of the disorder and subtle morphological alterations
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Neurofind was designed to make normative modelling accessible and therefore it is not customisable. Advanced users may prefer to have more control over certain aspects of the data and/or model training. In addition, Neurofind was developed to provide general purpose and transdiagnostic metrics that can be used across psychiatric and neurological research. It was not developed to identify specific disorders or predict clinical outcomes in a real-world clinical setting. To maintain simplicity and interpretability of the findings, the brain age model in Neurofind did not take its statistical dependency on chronological age into account. Because of this so-called ' regression to the mean ' or ' age bias ' , the ages of younger subjects tend to be overestimated, while the ages of older subjects tend to be underestimated. We recommend that any further analysis of brain age uses age as a covariate or addresses this issue in another way [95]. Neuroharmony, the method used to minimise the impact of scanner-related bias, relies on a learned association between image quality metrics and needed corrections. For Neuroharmony to work effectively, it is necessary that the quality metrics of the images fall within a certain range; conversely, Neuroharmony may not be able to predict the required adjustments if the quality metrics are unusual ... Neurofind may not be suitable for analysis of subjects that are very different from our training range, i.e., outside of ages 20 -80, non-white ethnicities, or MRI scans acquired with fields of strength considerably lower or higher than 1.5 T or 3 T. Finally, it is important to note that Neurofind is a research tool, so results should not be used to make clinical decisions.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study encourages researchers to always use Neurofind with patients alongside comparable healthy controls from their own sample to control for sample-specific biases; inferences should be made relative to this comparison group; the tool demonstrates capability for parsing heterogeneity through cosine similarity analysis of deviation patterns; successful application to disorders with different characteristics (AD with clear morphological markers versus SZ with subtle heterogeneous alterations) demonstrates tool flexibility; the web-based platform (www.neurofind.ai) provides automated processing from image upload to individualized PDF reports with minimal technical requirements; potential future applications include clustering patients by regional deviations, stratifying by longitudinal outcomes, or investigating associations with behavioral/cognitive/health traits in healthy controls

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is primarily a methods/tool development paper presenting Neurofind, a freely available web-based platform, rather than a traditional normative modeling research study. The tool wraps previously published methods (Neuroharmony for harmonization, AAE for outlier detection, SVR for brain age) into an accessible interface. Two independent normative models are provided: (1) Outlier Detection using AAE reconstruction error, and (2) Brain Age using SVR. The training data combined 4 publicly available datasets (HCP, HCP Aging, UK Biobank, IXI) with N=3362 after quality control and age restrictions (20-80 years). Validation was performed on 3 external clinical datasets (AIBL for AD, MCIC and COBRE for SZ) totaling N=364 participants. The tool outputs individualized reports as PDFs showing brain age, brain age gap, overall outlier index score with categorization, and regional deviations displayed on glass brain with full table. Scanner harmonization uses Neuroharmony which predicts ComBat-style corrections from image quality metrics, enabling harmonization of images from previously unseen scanners - a key innovation for clinical translation. The AAE architecture uses 101 input neurons (ROIs), encoder with 25 hidden neurons and 5-neuron latent code, conditioned on age and sex. Hyperparameters were optimized via grid search with 75/25 train/validation split, then final model trained on all training data. SVR used grid search over C parameter with 10-fold cross-validation, final C=2^-2. Code is available on GitHub. The exemplar applications successfully demonstrated the tool can identify meaningful deviations and parse heterogeneity, with AD showing expected patterns (temporal-limbic and ventricular involvement with high homogeneity) and SZ showing expected heterogeneity with subtle regional effects. Both conditions showed accelerated brain aging. The tool accepts NIfTI format images and performs all preprocessing automatically including FreeSurfer segmentation. Data imbalance was addressed by undersampling UK Biobank to maximum 55 participants per age group. Outlier removal was performed iteratively within each scanner (≥10 ROIs >3 SD from mean). Table S2 lists all 101 FreeSurfer regions extracted. The study represents an important step toward making normative modeling accessible to non-expert researchers in psychiatry and neurology.
